messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 73

# Clinical Vignette: Kofi, Age 50

Kofi has been a plumber for nearly twenty-five years. He knows how to read a building — the way pipes run hidden behind walls, the pressure that builds unseen until something gives. These days, he thinks about pressure a lot differently than he used to.

Eighteen months ago, Kofi was working late on a commercial job in an unfamiliar part of the city. He had stayed behind to finish a stubborn fitting while his crew left for the evening. Walking to his van in the parking structure, he was approached by two men. What followed happened fast — a demand for his tools and his keys, a refusal born of twenty-five years of hard work, and then a beating so severe that he was found an hour later by a security guard, his face unrecognizable, two ribs cracked, and his right hand — his working hand — fractured in three places.

He spent four days in hospital. His wife, Adwoa, sat beside him every night. He told her he was fine. He told himself the same thing.

He was back on the job in six weeks, earlier than his doctor advised. He needed to work. He needed to feel like himself again. But the man who returned to work was not quite the same man who had left.

The first thing Kofi notices, every single morning, is whether it is still dark outside. He will not leave the house before sunrise. He tells Adwoa it is about traffic, about timing, and she does not push him, though he can see in her face that she knows. At job sites, he positions himself so that his back is always to a wall. He has developed a habit of scanning every room he enters — doors, windows, exits — a ritual so automatic now that he barely registers doing it until a colleague catches him staring at nothing and asks if he is all right.

He is not all right. At night, he lies rigid beside Adwoa, listening to the building settle. When he does sleep, he is back in the parking structure. He can smell the concrete, the exhaust. He wakes soaked through, heart hammering, and sits on the edge of the bed in the dark for an hour, sometimes two, before his body believes it is over. Adwoa reaches for him during these episodes and he moves away — not from coldness, but because he cannot bear to be touched unexpectedly, even by her. This has put a distance between them that neither knows how to name.

At work, the hand healed well enough, but Kofi finds himself hesitating in ways he never did before. A colleague dropping a wrench on a concrete floor will send a spike of adrenaline through him so acute that he has to set down whatever he is holding and breathe through it. He has snapped at apprentices twice over small things and felt ashamed both times. He used to be known as the calm one, the one who could troubleshoot under pressure without raising his voice. That version of himself feels remote to him now, like someone he once knew.

He has stopped attending the Saturday morning football matches he played in for fifteen years. He has stopped going to the church he and Adwoa have attended since they arrived in this country. The thought of crowds, of being hemmed in, of having his back exposed, makes his chest tighten until he cannot think clearly. He tells people he has been busy. He is not busy. He is managing a radius of safety that keeps shrinking.

What troubles Kofi most, sitting in the quiet of his van before a job — the engine running, hands on the wheel — is not the fear itself but the arithmetic of it. He survived. He knows he survived. And yet some part of him, the part that still wakes at 3 a.m. in a cold sweat, does not seem to have received that information.
